chapters.title: Frameworks, formulas and unsaturation
chapters.formula: For hydrocarbons: DBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2
chapters.script: Welcome to Hydrocarbons. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen. Start with connectivity before choosing a reaction. An acyclic saturated alkane has two more hydrogen atoms than twice its carbon count. One ring or one double bond removes two hydrogens relative to that saturated reference; one triple bond removes four. The degree of unsaturation counts rings and pi bonds. For a neutral ordinary hydrocarbon, take twice the carbon count plus two, subtract the hydrogen count, and divide by two. Benzene's formula gives four, consistent with one ring and three pi bonds in a conventional contributor. The formula alone does not prove benzene: other connectivities can share it. Butane has zero degrees, butene has one, and butyne has two. In but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries two different groups, permitting geometrical isomers. A terminal double bond with two hydrogens on one carbon does not meet that requirement. Check valence, hydrogen count and possible stereoisomers before interpreting a formula as one unique molecule.
points: C₄H₁₀ · (10 − 10)/2 = 0 · Acyclic saturated
C₄H₈ · (10 − 8)/2 = 1 · One ring or C=C
C₆H₆ · (14 − 6)/2 = 4 · Formula ≠ unique shape

board.heading: Frameworks, formulas and unsaturation

chapters.title: Conformations and radical chains
chapters.formula: Initiation → propagation → termination
chapters.script: Rotation about ethane's carbon carbon single bond changes its conformation without changing which atoms are connected. In a Newman view along that bond, an eclipsed arrangement aligns front and back bonds, while a staggered arrangement offsets them. Staggered ethane has lower energy in the introductory model. These are conformations, not different constitutional isomers. Alkane chlorination under light changes connectivity through a radical chain. Initiation breaks a chlorine molecule homolytically to form two chlorine radicals. In propagation, a chlorine radical removes hydrogen from methane to give hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical. That methyl radical reacts with another chlorine molecule to form chloromethane and regenerate a chlorine radical. Each propagation sequence therefore maintains a reactive radical. Termination joins two radicals without generating another. Repeated substitution can form products beyond the first chlorinated compound, and unsymmetrical alkanes can give several positions of substitution. Product amounts depend on both how many hydrogens are available and their relative reaction rates. Do not predict product percentages from radical stability alone or assume all halogenations have identical selectivity.
points: Initiation · Cl₂ → 2 Cl• · Radicals created
Propagation · CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• · Radical regenerated
Termination · CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl · Radicals consumed

board.heading: Conformations and radical chains

chapters.title: Alkene orientation depends on pathway
chapters.formula: Propene + HBr: ionic and peroxide pathways differ
chapters.script: An alkene's pi electrons can begin bonding to an electrophile. In ordinary ionic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, protonation can lead toward a secondary or a primary carbocation. The pathway involving the more stable secondary intermediate is favoured, and bromide capture gives mainly two bromopropane. This is the familiar Markovnikov orientation for this substrate and these conditions. It is a result of a mechanism, not a direction rule independent of reagents. Carbocation rearrangements can change products in substrates where a more favourable intermediate is accessible. Suitable peroxide initiated radical conditions change the hydrogen bromide pathway. Bromine radical addition that forms the more stable carbon radical leads, after hydrogen abstraction, mainly to one bromopropane. The standard peroxide reversal applies to hydrogen bromide; it must not be transferred automatically to hydrogen chloride or hydrogen iodide. For every prediction write the alkene, reagent and radical or ionic conditions together. The carbon skeleton has three carbons in both propene products; the location of bromine changes, while no carbon is gained or lost.
points: HBr, ordinary conditions · Ionic addition · 2-bromopropane
HBr, suitable peroxides · Radical chain · 1-bromopropane
HCl or HI + peroxides · No general HBr shortcut · Check actual chemistry

board.heading: Alkene orientation depends on pathway

chapters.title: Hydrogenation, halogenation and hydration
chapters.formula: The solvent and catalyst help define the reaction
chapters.script: Adding hydrogen to an alkene with an appropriate metal catalyst converts its double bond into a single bond. Ethene becomes ethane, consuming one mole of hydrogen per mole of double bonds. Alkene bromination in a suitable non-nucleophilic medium commonly forms a vicinal dibromide, with bromine atoms on adjacent carbons. A bridged intermediate explains the usual anti addition rather than a freely rotating carbocation picture. If water is present, it can compete as a nucleophile and change the product toward a bromohydrin. Therefore a reagent name without solvent information may not fully specify the chemistry. Acid catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly propan two ol through the usual ionic orientation. Simply mixing an alkene with water does not imply rapid hydration without suitable conditions. In addition polymerization, many ethene molecules join as the pi bonds are replaced by bonds along a saturated chain. The polyethene repeat unit contains two carbon atoms each bearing two hydrogens. Distinguish a repeat unit from a whole polymer molecule.
points: Ethene · H₂; metal catalyst · Ethane
Alkene · Br₂; non-nucleophilic medium · Vicinal dibromide
Ethene · Polymerization conditions · [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ

chapters.title: Ozonolysis reconstructs double bonds
chapters.formula: Reductive work-up preserves aldehyde fragments
chapters.script: Ozonolysis is useful for locating an alkene double bond when the work-up is specified. Under reductive work-up, split the double bond and convert each of its carbons into a carbonyl carbon. Keep the other groups attached to that carbon. For but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries hydrogen and methyl, so each fragment is acetaldehyde, a two carbon aldehyde. One original molecule gives two acetaldehyde molecules. This result identifies the connectivity but does not by itself distinguish the geometrical isomers of but two ene. For two methylpropene, one double bonded carbon bears two methyl groups and gives propanone; the terminal carbon bears two hydrogens and gives formaldehyde, a one carbon aldehyde. Add the fragment carbon counts: three plus one returns the original four. A double bonded carbon with no hydrogen commonly yields a ketone fragment. A carbon bearing hydrogen can yield an aldehyde under the stated reductive conditions. Oxidative work-up can further change aldehyde products, so it must not be treated as interchangeable. Work backward by reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons when reconstructing a possible alkene.
points: But-2-ene · 2 ethanal · 2 + 2 = 4
2-Methylpropene · Propanone + methanal · 3 + 1 = 4

chapters.title: Alkynes: acidity and selective reduction
chapters.formula: Terminal sp C–H differs from an ordinary alkane C–H
chapters.script: A terminal alkyne has hydrogen directly attached to a carbon of the triple bond. Removing this hydrogen gives an acetylide ion. The greater s character of an sp orbital stabilizes the negative charge compared with comparable simple sp two or sp three carbanions. Terminal alkynes are consequently more acidic than comparable alkenes and alkanes, while remaining much weaker acids than water. A sufficiently strong base such as sodium amide can form an acetylide; aqueous hydroxide is not a quantitative substitute. Acetylides can form carbon carbon bonds with suitable unhindered primary alkyl halides by substitution, while more hindered substrates can favour elimination. Complete catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne consumes two equivalents of hydrogen to reach an alkane. Selective partial hydrogenation with a Lindlar catalyst can give a cis alkene from an appropriate internal alkyne. Dissolving metal reduction can instead give the trans alkene. The alkene formed from a terminal triple bond has a carbon bearing two hydrogens, so cis and trans labels do not apply. Reagents and equivalents decide how far the reduction proceeds.
points: Terminal C≡C–H · NaNH₂ · Acetylide formation
Internal alkyne · H₂; Lindlar catalyst · Cis alkene
Internal alkyne · Dissolving metal reduction · Trans alkene

chapters.title: Aromaticity and aromatic substitution
chapters.formula: Planar cyclic conjugation plus 4n + 2 π electrons
chapters.script: Benzene is a planar cyclic conjugated system with six pi electrons. It satisfies the introductory four n plus two aromatic electron rule with n equal to one. Electron count alone is insufficient: a molecule must also have the required cyclic conjugation and appropriate geometry. Benzene's carbon carbon bonds are equivalent; alternating bond drawings are contributors to a delocalized structure. In common electrophilic aromatic substitution, the ring forms a new bond to an electrophile and temporarily loses aromaticity. Removal of a proton restores the conjugated ring. Bromination commonly uses bromine with a Lewis acid such as iron three bromide. Nitration uses conditions that generate the nitronium electrophile. These ring substitutions replace a ring hydrogen and retain the six carbon framework. They differ from radical substitution on an alkyl side chain under light. In toluene, identify whether conditions target the aromatic ring or the benzylic position before assigning a product. Treat aromatic stabilization as an explanation for common reaction preferences, rather than a claim that an aromatic ring can never undergo any addition reaction.
points: Bromination · Br₂ with FeBr₃ · Ring H replaced

chapters.title: Directing groups and synthesis checks
chapters.formula: Activation and directing position are separate questions
chapters.script: A substituent influences both how rapidly an aromatic ring reacts and where a new group is introduced. An alkyl group generally activates the ring and favours ortho and para substitution. A nitro group deactivates the ring and favours meta substitution. Halogens are an important mixed case: they deactivate overall through electron withdrawal but direct toward ortho and para positions through resonance donation. A directing preference does not promise one pure positional product. Friedel Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group under suitable Lewis acid conditions, but rearrangements and repeated alkylation can complicate the result. Acylation introduces an acyl group and avoids the analogous carbocation skeleton rearrangement. Strongly deactivated rings and catalyst binding groups can prevent the usual reaction, so do not apply the name without checking the substrate. In a short synthesis, mark the reaction centre, count carbons, state the reagent and inspect competing pathways at each arrow. Use the practice questions to connect these choices rather than memorizing product names alone. More preparation routes and detailed stereochemical drawings remain useful.
points: Alkyl · Activating · Ortho / para
Nitro · Deactivating · Meta
Halogen · Deactivating · Ortho / para

chapters.title: Alkyne hydration gives carbonyl products
chapters.formula: Propyne: Hg²⁺/acid hydration → propanone; hydroboration–oxidation → propanal
chapters.script: Alkyne hydration usually requires following an initially formed enol to its carbonyl tautomer. An enol has hydroxyl attached to an alkene carbon; the final carbonyl product is not obtained by simply leaving that double bond unchanged. For propyne, aqueous acid with mercury two catalysis gives the Markovnikov hydration pattern and, after tautomerization, propanone. A suitable bulky borane followed by alkaline peroxide oxidation instead gives the terminal alkyne the complementary hydration orientation, leading to the aldehyde C H three, C H two, C H O, also called propionaldehyde. Both products retain the three carbon skeleton. They have the same molecular formula but different carbonyl positions and functional classes. Ethyne is an important special case: its acid catalysed hydration gives the aldehyde C H three, C H O, also called acetaldehyde, rather than a methyl ketone. Internal unsymmetrical alkynes can give product mixtures, so a terminal alkyne shortcut must not be applied indiscriminately. Read the catalyst and workup before selecting a product. Tautomerization moves a proton and changes bond placement; it is not merely resonance between drawings with the same hydrogen attachments. This distinction connects hydrocarbon reactions with the carbonyl chemistry developed in the Organic Oxygen class.
points: Propyne · Hg²⁺, aqueous acid · Propanone
Propyne · Bulky borane; oxidation · Propanal

chapters.title: Reconstruct an alkene from carbonyl fragments
chapters.formula: Reductive ozonolysis: join the two carbonyl carbons with C=C
chapters.script: Reductive ozonolysis can be read backward as well as forward. Each carbon of the original double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon while retaining its attached carbon groups. Suppose the products are one molecule of propanone and one of acetaldehyde, the two carbon aldehyde C H three, C H O. Propanone's carbonyl carbon carries two methyl groups. This aldehyde's carbonyl carbon carries one methyl group and one hydrogen. Join those two carbonyl carbons with a double bond and remove the carbonyl oxygens in the reconstruction. The original alkene is two methylbut two ene. It contains five carbons, matching three plus two in the products. This reconstruction determines connectivity, but carbonyl fragments alone do not generally recover an alkene's original E or Z geometry. In this particular alkene, two identical methyl groups on one double bonded carbon prevent E and Z isomerism. The workup matters: oxidative ozonolysis can further oxidize aldehyde products, changing the evidence used for reconstruction. State reductive conditions before treating an aldehyde as the final fragment. Finish by counting carbon atoms and checking which double bonded carbon had a hydrogen.
points: Fragment 1 · Propanone · Two methyl groups
Fragment 2 · Ethanal · Methyl and H
Reconstructed alkene · Join carbonyl carbons · 2-methylbut-2-ene

chapters.title: Check aromaticity before counting alone
chapters.formula: Cyclic, planar, continuously conjugated; 4n + 2 π electrons
chapters.script: Aromaticity in the simple Hückel model requires more than a special electron count. The ring must be cyclic, approximately planar and continuously conjugated, with a suitable p orbital at each position. A closed shell ring with four n plus two pi electrons can then be aromatic. Benzene has six pi electrons, corresponding to n equal to one. The cyclopentadienyl anion also has six: four from two double bonds and two from the relevant lone pair in its conjugated ring. The cycloheptatrienyl cation has six pi electrons from three double bonds and an empty p orbital at the cationic position. Charge alone therefore does not prohibit aromaticity. A planar fully conjugated four pi electron ring instead fits the antiaromatic pattern. A nonplanar molecule that avoids continuous effective overlap may be nonaromatic rather than antiaromatic, even if a naive count gives four n electrons. Cyclooctatetraene is the familiar nonplanar example. Always check geometry and conjugation before applying the electron rule. The model here concerns simple monocyclic systems and is not a universal classification shortcut for every fused or unusual structure.
points: Benzene · Planar conjugated ring · 6 π; aromatic
Cyclopentadienyl anion · Lone pair participates · 6 π; aromatic
Cyclooctatetraene · Nonplanar ground state · Nonaromatic

chapters.title: Separate directing effects from activation
chapters.formula: Halogens: deactivating yet ortho/para-directing in electrophilic substitution
chapters.script: An existing substituent affects both how fast an aromatic ring reacts and where a new group preferentially enters. Those are separate questions. Relative to carbon one bearing the substituent, carbons two and six are ortho, three and five are meta, and carbon four is para. A methyl group commonly activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution and favours ortho and para products. A nitro group strongly deactivates and favours meta substitution. Halogens are the important combination: they deactivate the ring overall but still direct predominantly ortho and para. Their inductive withdrawal and resonance donation influence different aspects of the comparison. Do not infer that an ortho para director must always make the ring more reactive than benzene. Nor does directing preference promise one pure product. Steric effects, electrophile, medium and additional substituents can affect the product mixture. The labelled rings show relative positions rather than exact yields. For several substituents, compare their competing effects and blocked sites before predicting the next position. Keep electrophilic ring substitution distinct from radical reaction at an alkyl side chain.
points: Methyl substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Activating; ortho/para
Nitro substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Deactivating; meta
Halogen substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Deactivating; ortho/para

chapters.title: Benzylic reactions need the right site
chapters.formula: Side-chain oxidation usually requires at least one benzylic H
chapters.script: The benzylic carbon is directly attached to an aromatic ring. Its chemistry differs from that of a carbon bearing hydrogen within the ring itself. Under the usual strong side chain oxidation conditions, an alkylbenzene with at least one benzylic hydrogen can yield a carboxyl group at the ring attachment, followed by acid workup. Toluene and ethylbenzene therefore both give benzoic acid in that introductory comparison. The extra carbon in ethylbenzene does not become a longer carboxylic acid side chain. Carbon lost from the side chain must be accounted for in a full balanced oxidation, rather than silently assumed to remain in the main organic product. Tert butylbenzene has no hydrogen on its benzylic carbon and does not follow this ordinary side chain oxidation shortcut. Radical halogenation under suitable light or radical initiating conditions can also target benzylic positions, whereas electrophilic aromatic halogenation uses a different pathway and catalyst context. Identify the reacting carbon, the presence of its hydrogen and the reagent conditions before deciding whether the ring or side chain changes.
points: Toluene · Benzylic H present · Benzoic acid after workup

chapters.title: Hydrogen uptake does not count every ring
chapters.formula: A simple C₆H₁₀ skeleton has DBE 2; hydrogenation evidence needs a reaction model
chapters.script: Molecular formula and hydrogen uptake provide complementary evidence, rather than a unique structure by themselves. For an ordinary neutral hydrocarbon with six carbons and ten hydrogens, the degree of unsaturation is two. One ring and one double bond, two double bonds, or one triple bond can each account for that value. Now suppose a supplied hydrogenation model saturates ordinary carbon carbon multiple bonds while retaining the carbon skeleton and not opening rings. A cycloalkene with one ring and one double bond consumes one mole hydrogen per mole molecule, giving a saturated monocyclic hydrocarbon. An acyclic diene consumes two, while an acyclic alkyne also consumes two on complete reduction to the alkane. Thus two moles hydrogen uptake cannot distinguish a diene from an alkyne without additional evidence. A ring contributes to the formula based unsaturation count even when it does not consume hydrogen in the stated reaction model. Real catalyst and substrate chemistry can be more complicated, especially for strained rings or aromatic systems, so the restriction is essential. Count formula units, reactive multiple bonds and structural possibilities separately before claiming that one measurement identifies a unique hydrocarbon.
points: C₆H₁₀ · DBE = (2×6+2−10)/2 · 2 unsaturation units
One ring + one C=C · Saturate C=C; ring retained · 1 mol H₂ per mol molecule

chapters.title: Terminal alkyne alkylation joins carbon fragments
chapters.formula: Acetylide + suitable primary alkyl halide → a new C–C bond
chapters.script: A terminal alkyne can form a carbon nucleophile after its terminal proton is removed in a suitable acid base step. In the elementary acetylide alkylation model, that carbon nucleophile attacks a suitable primary alkyl halide through substitution and makes a new carbon carbon bond. Consider the anion derived from ethyne and an ethyl halide. The two carbon acetylide fragment joins the two carbon ethyl fragment, giving a four carbon alkyne, but one yne. The triple bond remains; substitution replaces the halide on the alkyl partner rather than hydrogenating the alkyne. Starting instead with the three carbon terminal alkyne propyne and a methyl halide gives the four carbon internal alkyne but two yne. The location of the triple bond follows the connectivity of the joined fragments, not just their total carbon count. Secondary and tertiary alkyl halides can favour elimination with a strongly basic acetylide, so they are not interchangeable with a suitable primary substrate in a simple selective route. Proton donors can also consume the acetylide. Treat these examples as reaction planning and carbon ledgers under the stated model, not as instructions for preparing or handling the reagent.
points: Ethyne-derived C₂ fragment · Join an ethyl C₂ fragment · But-1-yne: 4 carbons

chapters.title: Addition polymers preserve the monomer atom inventory
chapters.formula: n CH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]n: no small-molecule loss in the ideal addition step
chapters.script: Addition polymerization changes how monomer units are connected without requiring a water molecule to be removed from every link. In the ideal ethene example, the carbon carbon double bond opens into chain connectivity and each repeat unit retains the monomer's two carbons and four hydrogens. The repeat unit mass is approximately twenty eight grams per mole using the supplied integer atomic masses. If a hypothetical chain has molar mass twenty eight thousand grams per mole and end group masses are neglected, its degree of polymerization is about one thousand repeat units. That is not one thousand carbon atoms: the repeat units together contain about two thousand carbons. One mole of such ideal chains represents about one thousand moles of incorporated monomer units. Real polymer samples contain a distribution of chain lengths, and a reported average molar mass must be interpreted with its averaging convention. Initiator fragments, end groups, branching and unreacted monomer can affect actual mass accounting. The elementary repeat unit calculation therefore supplies an approximate chain size under stated assumptions, rather than proving that every molecule in a sample has exactly the same length or that a condensation water loss should be subtracted.
points: Ethene repeat unit · C₂H₄; supplied mass 28 g/mol · No link-by-link H₂O loss

chapters.title: Two substituents can reinforce or conflict in direction
chapters.formula: Number the ring before combining directing preferences
chapters.script: A disubstituted aromatic ring requires combining the effects of both existing groups. Consider a ring numbered with a methyl group at carbon one and a carboxyl group at carbon four. In the usual introductory electrophilic substitution comparison, methyl favours ortho and para positions relative to itself. Its free ortho positions are two and six, while its para position is already occupied. The carboxyl group is a meta director, and positions two and six are also meta to carbon four. Thus both preferences point toward the same two symmetry related sites in this example. Positions two and six describe the same constitutional monoproduct after the appropriate ring symmetry is considered, rather than two guaranteed different products. This agreement does not mean the ring reacts faster than benzene overall or that all other products are impossible. The electron withdrawing group can reduce reactivity, and the observed selectivity depends on conditions. If two groups favour different sites, their relative influence and steric effects need to be considered instead of applying a mechanical one group rule. State the numbering, occupied positions and symmetry.
points: CH₃ at ring position 1 · Ortho preference; para occupied · Free preferred sites 2 and 6
COOH at position 4 · Meta preference · Sites 2 and 6 agree

chapters.title: Hydroboration changes hydration orientation
chapters.formula: Propene: acid hydration → propan-2-ol; hydroboration–oxidation → propan-1-ol
chapters.script: Two alkene hydration routes can give different alcohols while retaining the same carbon skeleton. In ordinary acid catalysed hydration of propene, the hydroxyl group appears mainly on the central carbon, giving propan two ol. Hydroboration followed by suitable oxidation instead gives propan one ol, placing the hydroxyl group on the less substituted terminal carbon. During hydroboration, boron and hydrogen add from the same face of the double bond. Oxidation replaces the carbon boron bond with a carbon oxygen bond with retention at that carbon, so the overall addition of hydrogen and hydroxyl is syn. This is a stereochemical statement, while the less substituted carbon preference is a regiochemical statement. Neither should be confused with the radical peroxide effect for hydrogen bromide. The hydroboration step does not proceed through a free carbocation, so the familiar carbocation rearrangement argument is not the pathway used here. Both propene products have three carbons and the alcohol formula three carbons, eight hydrogens and one oxygen. Their different hydroxyl positions make them constitutional isomers. Always name both the reagent sequence and the product connectivity before applying an orientation label.

chapters.title: Oxidative cleavage depends on carbon substitution
chapters.formula: Strong alkene oxidation, then acid workup: =CH₂ → CO₂; =CHR → RCOOH; =CR₂ → ketone
chapters.script: Cleavage of an alkene does not always stop at the same products as reductive ozonolysis. Under the standard strong oxidative cleavage model using hot permanganate with an appropriate acid workup, examine each original double bonded carbon separately. A carbon carrying one hydrogen gives a carboxylic acid fragment. A carbon carrying no hydrogen gives a ketone fragment. A terminal methylene carbon can be oxidized through smaller intermediates to carbon dioxide in the complete oxidation model. Thus propene gives ethanoic acid and carbon dioxide after the specified workup, accounting for two organic carbons plus one inorganic carbon. Two methylbut two ene instead gives propanone and ethanoic acid: its more substituted double bond carbon becomes a ketone and its hydrogen bearing partner becomes an acid. The total carbon count remains five. Cold dilute permanganate under mild conditions can instead favour addition to form a vicinal diol, so the reagent name alone does not fix the oxidation extent. Carboxylate salts can be present before acid workup. State conditions and workup before choosing between diol formation, aldehyde formation and further oxidative cleavage.

chapters.title: Hydrogenation enthalpy compares starting alkenes
chapters.formula: Same hydrogenation product: H(A) − H(B) = ΔHhyd(B) − ΔHhyd(A)
chapters.script: Hydrogenation energy can compare two starting alkenes only when the reaction endpoints are properly matched. Suppose two isomeric alkenes each consume one mole of hydrogen to form the same alkane in the same physical state. Use illustrative hydrogenation enthalpies of minus one hundred twenty kilojoules per mole for A and minus one hundred sixteen for B. Because both routes finish at the same enthalpy, A must start four kilojoules per mole above B. It releases more heat because its initial enthalpy is higher, so B is the more enthalpically stable alkene in this comparison. The less negative hydrogenation enthalpy therefore corresponds to the lower starting enthalpy when the endpoints match. This does not establish which alkene hydrogenates faster: activation barriers control reaction rates. It also does not directly provide an equilibrium constant, which depends on Gibbs energy and therefore includes entropy. Comparing different product alkanes without correcting their enthalpies would invalidate the simple subtraction. In exam data, first verify equal reaction stoichiometry and a common final product, then subtract the signed enthalpies before interpreting stability.

chapters.title: Mixed Wurtz coupling gives several skeletons
chapters.formula: RBr + R′Br + sodium: R–R, R–R′ and R′–R′ are possible couplings
chapters.script: The Wurtz reaction illustrates why a carbon joining reaction is not automatically a selective synthesis. In the simple net model, two alkyl bromide molecules react with two sodium atoms to give one coupled alkane and two sodium bromide units. With only a suitable primary ethyl halide, the carbon groups can join to give butane. Now consider a mixture of methyl and ethyl halides. Methyl with methyl gives ethane, methyl with ethyl gives propane, and ethyl with ethyl gives butane. The cross coupled product is therefore accompanied by two possible self coupling skeletons. Listing those three products does not prove that they occur in equal amounts, or that the desired cross product has a fixed yield. Reactivity, competing reactions and conditions affect the actual mixture. The mixed route is consequently a poor general way to claim selective preparation of an unsymmetrical alkane. Carbon accounting still provides a reliable check: combine the carbon counts of the two groups that actually join, rather than adding all the starting carbons into every product. Treat the net equation as transformation bookkeeping and keep selectivity separate from theoretical stoichiometry.

chapters.title: Anti addition distinguishes meso from racemic products
chapters.formula: trans-But-2-ene → meso dibromide; cis-but-2-ene → (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair in the ideal anti model
chapters.script: Stereospecific addition can preserve information about an alkene's starting geometry. Consider the usual bromonium mediated anti addition to but two ene in a suitable non nucleophilic medium. The trans alkene gives meso two three dibromobutane, with opposite configurations at its two stereogenic carbons and internal symmetry. The cis alkene instead gives the two enantiomeric configurations two R three R and two S three S in equal amounts under achiral conditions. The meso product and the racemic mixture can both show zero net optical rotation, but for different reasons. A meso molecule is achiral despite containing stereogenic centres; a racemic sample contains chiral molecules whose rotations cancel. Do not identify these outcomes merely from the word anti, since chain rotation can change a product drawing without changing its configuration. Track the initial alkene geometry and the three dimensional addition together. Both transformations retain four carbons and add two bromines, giving the same constitutional dibromide formula. A competing nucleophile such as water can change the functional product, so this comparison assumes the stated dibromide pathway.

chapters.title: Strong alkyne cleavage counts both triple-bond carbons
chapters.formula: Pent-2-yne → C2 acid + C3 acid; pent-1-yne → C4 acid + CO₂ in the stated oxidation model
chapters.script: Strong oxidative cleavage of an alkyne does not give the same products as its ordinary hydration. In a supplied cleavage model, each carbon of an internal triple bond becomes a carboxyl carbon in one fragment after the stated acidic workup. Pent two yne therefore gives ethanoic acid with two carbons and propanoic acid with three. The triple bond divided the five carbon chain into those two pieces; no extra carbon entered with oxygen. For pent one yne, the terminal triple bond carbon instead reaches carbon dioxide in the complete oxidation model, while the other fragment is four carbon butanoic acid. Counting only the isolated organic acid would miss one starting carbon. Compare these outcomes with a hydration map, which retains all five carbons in one carbonyl product rather than cleaving the skeleton. Actual oxidation can be more complex and yields need not be quantitative, so the named products belong to the stated ideal cleavage endpoint. Mark both original triple bond carbons before naming the fragments, and include inorganic carbon products when checking total carbon conservation.

chapters.title: Aromatic sulfonation is a reversible substitution map
chapters.formula: C₆H₆ + SO₃ ⇌ C₆H₅SO₃H; substitution changes a ring H, not the carbon skeleton
chapters.script: Aromatic sulfonation is a useful exception to treating every substitution arrow as irreversible. In the conceptual benzene and sulfur trioxide map, a ring hydrogen is replaced by a sulfonic acid group while the six carbon framework remains intact. Sulfur trioxide and strongly acidic sulfonating media favour the forward transformation; suitable hot dilute aqueous acidic conditions can favour removal of the sulfonic group and return a ring hydrogen. The overall direction depends on the specified medium and equilibrium, not just on recognizing a named reaction. A sulfonic acid group deactivates the ring and is usually meta directing toward further electrophilic substitution. It can also occupy a position temporarily in a supporting synthesis plan, but removal requires a separate stated transformation. Do not confuse sulfonation with attaching an alkyl group or with a sulfone containing two carbon groups on sulfur. The formula benzene plus sulfur trioxide balances without losing carbon or generating an extra ring. This is a functional group and reversibility comparison, not a set of experimental preparation conditions or a promise that every substituted aromatic substrate follows the same selective pathway.

chapters.title: Combustion gas volumes can determine a hydrocarbon formula
chapters.formula: CxHy uses x+y/4 volumes O₂ and forms x volumes CO₂ per volume hydrocarbon
chapters.script: Supplied gas volume data can identify a molecular formula under carefully stated assumptions. Consider twenty millilitres of one pure gaseous hydrocarbon mixed with one hundred thirty millilitres of oxygen. Complete combustion is followed by cooling so water condenses. At the same comparison temperature and pressure, the remaining gas volume is ninety millilitres. A separate selective carbon dioxide absorption leaves thirty millilitres of oxygen. Thus carbon dioxide occupied sixty millilitres and oxygen consumed was one hundred. Dividing by the original hydrocarbon volume gives three carbon dioxide volumes and five oxygen volumes per hydrocarbon volume. In the equation for carbon x hydrogen y, carbon dioxide coefficient is x and oxygen coefficient is x plus y over four. Therefore x is three and y is eight: the supplied hydrocarbon is propane. The cooled ninety millilitres is not pure carbon dioxide because excess oxygen remains. The calculation assumes only the stated gases, complete combustion, selective absorption and negligible residual water vapour. It is interpretation of idealized observations, not an instruction to ignite a gas mixture.

chapters.title: Radical product proportions count sites and per-hydrogen reactivity
chapters.formula: Propane: 6 primary H and 2 secondary H; supplied ksecondary/kprimary=4 ⇒ weights 6:8 ⇒ products 3:4
chapters.script: The more reactive type of hydrogen does not automatically supply the product ratio by itself. Consider an original low conversion monochlorination model for propane. Its two equivalent methyl ends contain six primary hydrogens in total, and its middle carbon contains two secondary hydrogens. Suppose the supplied relative abstraction rate per secondary hydrogen is four, while that per primary hydrogen is one under the stated conditions. Multiply the number of each type of hydrogen by its per hydrogen reactivity. The primary substitution channel has weight six times one, or six. The secondary channel has weight two times four, or eight. Normalize by the total fourteen to obtain three sevenths one chloropropane and four sevenths two chloropropane, approximately forty two point nine and fifty seven point one percent. The two equivalent chain ends give the same primary constitutional product. Neither the raw six to two hydrogen count nor the bare one to four reactivity ratio is the final product ratio. The value four is supplied for this exercise, not a universal chlorination constant. Repeated substitution, changing conditions and substantial conversion can invalidate the simple two channel estimate.

chapters.title: Syn hydroxylation gives a different stereochemical map from anti addition
chapters.formula: Ideal syn OH addition: cis-but-2-ene→meso butane-2,3-diol; trans→(2R,3R)+(2S,3S) under achiral conditions
chapters.script: Two reactions that add groups to the same double bond can produce different stereochemical outcomes because their addition geometries differ. Use an ideal stereospecific syn hydroxylation of but two ene, meaning both oxygen groups are delivered from the same alkene face and then appear as adjacent hydroxyl groups after the stated workup. The carbon skeleton stays intact and the product is butane two three diol. Starting from the cis alkene gives the meso configuration, with opposite R and S centres; its alternative R S and S R labels describe the same molecule under the end to end symmetry. Starting from the trans alkene gives the R R and S S enantiomer pair when both faces react equally under achiral conditions. Compare this with the earlier anti bromination map: the stereochemical relationship is reversed. Do not transfer the word meso from one reaction to another without checking syn versus anti delivery and the actual substituents. Both a meso sample and an exactly racemic sample can have zero net optical rotation for different reasons. These statements assume the specified stereospecific pathway, an achiral environment and no later stereochemical scrambling; they are not a claim that every oxidizing condition gives an intact diol.

chapters.title: Cleaving a cyclic double bond can leave one connected molecule
chapters.formula: Cyclohexene + reductive ozonolysis ⇒ OHC–(CH₂)₄–CHO; one hexane-1,6-dial per ring
chapters.script: Breaking a double bond does not always split an organic molecule into two separate molecules. Consider cyclohexene with one double bond between labelled ring carbons one and two. In reductive ozonolysis, remove the bond between those two carbons and replace each double bonded carbon by a carbonyl carbon while retaining its other original neighbours. Each alkene carbon originally bears a hydrogen, so each becomes an aldehyde end under the stated reductive workup. The remaining path through carbons three, four, five and six still connects the two former double bond carbons. The product is therefore a single six carbon chain with an aldehyde at each end: hexane one six dial, written O H C, four methylene groups, then C H O. Its formula is carbon six hydrogen ten oxygen two. One mole of the starting monocyclic alkene gives one mole of this dialdehyde in the ideal quantitative map, not two moles of three carbon aldehyde. The ring has opened, but the carbon inventory remains six. Further oxidation can convert aldehyde ends to acids, so the workup must be stated. More complicated polycyclic substrates require tracing every remaining carbon connection rather than applying a universal two fragment rule.

chapters.title: An electrophilic addition can rearrange before halide capture
chapters.formula: CH₂=CH–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ + HCl: secondary C2 cation → 1,2-H shift → tertiary C3 cation → rearranged chloride
chapters.script: An orientation rule for proton addition is not the last step when a carbocation can rearrange. Use three methylbut one ene with its four carbon chain labelled one through four and a methyl branch at carbon three. In a conventional ionic hydrogen chloride addition description, proton attachment at terminal carbon one leaves a secondary carbocation at carbon two. A neighbouring carbon three hydrogen can migrate with its bond pair to carbon two, moving the positive site to carbon three and giving a tertiary carbocation. Chloride capture there yields the rearranged connectivity two chloro two methylbutane after renumbering the product. Direct capture before the shift instead gives the unrearranged connectivity two chloro three methylbutane. Both retain five carbons and have formula carbon five hydrogen eleven chlorine. Their relative amounts depend on competing pathways; a stability comparison alone does not justify declaring a single quantitative product. This is a specified ionic H C l example, not the peroxide initiated hydrogen bromide chain mechanism. Track the labelled carbons through protonation, hydrogen migration and capture before renumbering the final name. The migrating hydrogen carries an electron pair; no carbon atom or free hydride reagent is inserted.
